course_title: Microsoft Certified: Azure Database Administrator Associate (DP-300)
chapter_summary:
The migration of your database to Azure is not complete until thorough post-migration optimization and validation have been performed. This critical phase ensures that your data is intact, your applications function correctly, and your database performs optimally in its new cloud environment. Skipping these steps can lead to data inconsistencies, application errors, and unexpected performance issues, undermining the benefits of cloud migration.

The first step in post-migration is **data integrity validation**. This involves comparing data between the source and target databases to ensure no data loss or corruption occurred during the transfer. For smaller datasets, you might perform row counts on key tables or checksum comparisons. For larger databases, sampling techniques or specialized data comparison tools can be used. For example, if you migrated a SQL Server database, you could run `CHECKSUM TABLE` on both source and target, or write T-SQL queries to compare row counts and aggregate values (like `SUM` or `AVG`) for critical columns. For PostgreSQL, similar aggregate queries or `pg_checksums` (though primarily for physical integrity) can be used. It's also crucial to validate schema objects – ensuring all tables, views, stored procedures, functions, and indexes are present and correctly defined in the target.

Once data integrity is confirmed, **application functionality testing** is paramount. Update your application's connection strings to point to the new Azure database endpoint. This typically involves changing the server name, port, and potentially credentials. For example, a SQL Server connection string might change from `Server=myonpremiseserver;...` to `Server=myazuresqlserver.database.windows.net;...`. After updating, run a full suite of application tests, including unit tests, integration tests, and user acceptance tests (UAT). Pay close attention to any queries that previously performed well but are now slow, or any application features that behave unexpectedly. This is where performance tuning comes into play.

**Performance optimization** in Azure often involves adjusting server parameters that might differ from your on-premises configuration. For Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance, this could mean reviewing service tiers, vCore counts, and max degree of parallelism (MAXDOP) settings. For Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL, you'll delve into server parameters like `shared_buffers`, `work_mem`, `effective_cache_size` for PostgreSQL, or `innodb_buffer_pool_size`, `query_cache_size` for MySQL. Rebuilding or reorganizing indexes and updating statistics (`UPDATE STATISTICS` in SQL Server, `ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL/MySQL) are fundamental tasks to ensure the query optimizer has accurate information for generating efficient execution plans.

```sql
-- Example for SQL Server: Rebuild an index
ALTER INDEX ALL ON <TableName> REBUILD;
UPDATE STATISTICS <TableName>;

-- Example for PostgreSQL: Reanalyze a table
ANALYZE <TableName>;

-- Example for MySQL: Optimize a table (rebuilds indexes and reclaims space)
OPTIMIZE TABLE <TableName>;
```

**Security hardening** is equally vital. Configure Azure network security settings, such as Virtual Network (VNet) integration, Private Link, and firewall rules, to restrict access to your database. Implement appropriate authentication methods (e.g., Azure Active Directory authentication for Azure SQL, or strong password policies for all databases) and configure authorization using roles and permissions. Review existing logins and users, ensuring only necessary accounts have access and that their permissions adhere to the principle of least privilege.

Finally, establish **ongoing monitoring and alerting** using Azure Monitor, Azure Log Analytics, and specific database monitoring tools (e.g., Query Performance Insight for Azure SQL). Configure alerts for critical metrics like CPU utilization, I/O latency, storage usage, and failed logins. This proactive monitoring helps detect and address performance issues or security threats before they impact your applications. A common mistake is assuming that cloud services automatically handle all performance tuning; while Azure provides a robust platform, database-level optimization is still your responsibility as an administrator. Always document your post-migration configurations and changes for future reference and disaster recovery planning.

screens.title: Post-migration Optimization and Validation
screens.subtitle: Make sure your migrated database is correct, secure, and performing in Azure.

narration.text: You’ve completed the migration, but the work isn’t over. In this lesson you’ll learn how to validate that data and schema arrived intact, confirm application functionality, tune performance for the cloud, and harden access so your Azure database is secure. We’ll cover practical checks you can run, commands you’ll use to update statistics and rebuild indexes, how to adjust server parameters or scale the service tier, and where to configure network protections like VNet or Private Link. You’ll also see how to wire up monitoring and alerts so issues surface before users report them. A concrete example you’ll practice is running update statistics and a rebuild on a sample table, then using a missing index DMV to identify candidates for new indexes. A common misconception is that cloud services automatically tune everything; in reality, database-level validation and optimization remain your responsibility. At the end of the module you will know which tools and steps to take to prove integrity, restore performance, and maintain security for your migrated database. What will you validate first when you inspect a migrated database?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Post-migration work proves correctness, restores performance, and secures access. Validation plus targeted tuning makes the migration successful in production.

Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Post-migration Optimization and Validation
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Post-migration Optimization and Validation

This module teaches the checks and changes you must run after migration to ensure data integrity, application correctness, performance tuning, and security hardening in Azure.

Orientation

We move from verifying that the data copied correctly to tuning indexes and parameters, then lock down network and authentication, and finally set up monitoring and alerts for ongoing operations.

Explore Key Topics
Data Integrity
Compare row counts, aggregates, or checksums to prove data moved without loss or corruption.
Performance Tuning
Rebuild indexes, update statistics, and review server parameters or service tier for cloud workloads.
Security & Monitoring
Enforce VNet or Private Link, use role-based permissions, and configure alerts for CPU, I/O, and failed logins.
Visual checklist
A compact view of validation, tuning, and security steps to track progress.
Validate data
Row counts, checksums, and sampled aggregates.
Test apps
Update connection strings and run unit, integration, and UAT tests.
Tune & secure
Index maintenance, stats, server settings, VNet or Private Link, and alerts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to perform step-by-step post-migration validation and optimization in Azure. First, you will run data integrity checks to confirm no records were lost or corrupted during transfer, using row counts, checksums, or sampled aggregates for large datasets. Second, you will update application connection strings and run unit, integration, and acceptance tests to prove that the application works against the new Azure endpoint. Third, you will tune database performance by rebuilding indexes and updating statistics, and by reviewing server parameters or scaling the service tier to match workload needs. Fourth, you will secure the database with network controls like VNet or Private Link, proper firewall rules, and role-based authentication. Each of these skills ensures the migration is not just complete, but reliable and maintainable. Practice the verification steps and document your changes so future administrators can reproduce them. Which objective will you prioritize in your next migration?

keyIdea.text: Verify data and app functionality, tune performance, and harden security as core post-migration tasks you must own.

screens.title: Post-migration validation — an overview
screens.subtitle: Define the end-state that proves a successful migration

narration.text: Post-migration validation is the set of checks and tests you run after data has been moved to Azure to prove that the system is correct, functional, and ready to operate. At its core, validation confirms three things: the data arrived intact, the application behaves correctly against the new endpoint, and performance is acceptable for user workloads. A simple example is running row-count comparisons on critical tables and executing a sample transaction from the application to verify both data and behavior. A common misconception is that a successful data transfer log or a green status in a migration tool means the application is ready. It does not. Tools can confirm bytes copied, but they cannot prove query plans, index usage, or network access. Validation bridges that gap by including schema checks, query performance spot-checks, and connectivity tests. In practice you will create a short checklist for each database that includes data integrity checks, schema object verification, application test cases, and initial performance baselining. Treat this checklist as evidence for go/no-go decisions. Before you move to tuning and hardening, ask: which business-critical queries must meet response-time targets in production?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Validation proves data integrity, application functionality, and acceptable performance after migration.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Post-migration validation — an overview
What validation looks like
  • Data integrity: row counts, checksums, or sampled aggregates for large tables.
  • Schema verification: confirm tables, views, procedures, functions, and indexes exist and match definitions.
  • Application connectivity: update connection strings and run test suites to exercise business flows.
  • Performance spot checks: baseline critical queries and record metrics for comparison.
Why it matters

Validation prevents surprises in production by proving the database and application behave as expected before full cutover.

Concrete checklist card
Data check
Compare row counts for key tables and validate sums for monetary columns as a quick evidence set.
App test
Run a UAT script that exercises top user transactions and observes response times and errors.
Takeaway
Validation is the gate that turns a migrated database into a production-ready system.
Common mistake

Relying solely on migration tool success or logs; always run independent verification queries and tests.

screens.title: Data integrity validation methods
screens.subtitle: Prove that every record and value arrived unchanged

narration.text: Data integrity validation uses deterministic and sampling techniques to prove no data was lost or corrupted during migration. For small datasets, deterministic checks such as row counts and checksums are quick and conclusive. For larger databases, full checksums may be impractical, so you use sampling: compare aggregates like total sums or averages for key columns, and run checks on representative partitions. The chapter suggests commands and approaches you can use with S Q L Server, PostgreSQL, and MySQL. For example, you might run a checksum or aggregate on a critical table and compare the result between source and target. Another useful check is to compare counts grouped by key columns to catch partial copies. A concrete example is computing SUM of an amount column on an orders table before and after migration; differing totals point to missing or truncated rows. A common misconception is that identical row counts guarantee identical data. Counts hide value-level corruption; include column-level aggregates and hash checks where possible. After validation, record the queries and outputs so you can prove integrity to stakeholders. Data integrity validation methods means use row counts, checksums, aggregates, and sampling to validate data integrity at scale.. In practical terms, prove that every record and value arrived unchanged. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Methods
keyIdea.text: Use row counts, checksums, aggregates, and sampling to validate data integrity at scale.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Data integrity validation methods
Techniques
  • Deterministic: full checksums or row counts for small to medium tables.
  • Sampling: aggregates and partitioned checks for very large tables.
  • Column-level checks: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX to detect value-level differences.
  • Schema object presence: ensure tables and indexes exist as expected.
Key takeaway

Combine counts with value aggregates to detect omissions and corruption.

Concrete examples (visual)
-- SQL Server: checksum or aggregated sum
SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows, SUM(TotalAmount) AS total_sum FROM Sales.Orders;

-- PostgreSQL: aggregate sample
SELECT COUNT(*), AVG(quantity), SUM(amount) FROM public.orders WHERE order_date > '2023-01-01';

-- MySQL: optimize or analyze table after validation
ANALYZE TABLE orders;
Note: these queries are evidence items to record; do not rely on a single check.
Misconception

Identical row counts alone do not guarantee identical values. Include column-level checks or checksums for critical fields.

screens.title: Schema and object verification
screens.subtitle: Ensure tables, views, indexes, and routines were migrated correctly

narration.text: Schema and object verification makes sure that not only the rows but also the database structure arrived and behaves as expected. This includes confirming that tables, views, stored procedures, functions, triggers, and indexes exist in the target and match the source definitions. A practical approach is to script object definitions from the source and compare them to the target, or to run catalog queries that list objects and their properties. For example, compare index names and included columns to detect missing or altered indexes. Missing indexes can change query plans dramatically, so verifying index presence is critical. Another check is to run a small suite that executes stored procedures and functions to catch runtime errors caused by dependency changes or permission differences. A common mistake is assuming that object names alone are sufficient; you must verify definitions and permissions too. Document any differences and decide whether to recreate objects, alter definitions, or adjust application queries. Verifying schema objects prevents subtle behavioral changes that only surface under load. Schema and object verification means check object definitions, index structures, and runtime behavior of stored routines to avoid hidden functional regressions.. In practical terms, ensure tables, views, indexes, and routines were migrated correctly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Schema verification
keyIdea.text: Check object definitions, index structures, and runtime behavior of stored routines to avoid hidden functional regressions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Schema and object verification
Checklist
  • Compare table and column definitions between source and target.
  • Verify index names, keys, included columns, and uniqueness constraints.
  • Confirm stored procedures and functions compile and run expected inputs.
  • Check permissions and logins for least-privilege access.
Example

Script the definition of a stored procedure on the source, compare to the target, and run a smoke invocation to verify behavior.

Concrete verification card
Index check
List indexes and compare column lists and sizes; missing index columns often cause plan regressions.
Permissions
Validate that application logins map to appropriate users and roles on the target server.
Common mistake

Only checking object names; always compare full definitions and test runtime behavior to be safe.

screens.title: Update connection strings and test application functionality
screens.subtitle: Prove the application works end-to-end with the Azure database

narration.text: Updating connection strings and exercising your application are essential to prove functionality after migration. Connection strings typically change the server name, port, or authentication method. For example, a S Q L Server connection string moves from an on-premises host to an Azure S Q L endpoint that includes the database server DNS name. After you change the connection string in a controlled environment, run your unit tests, integration tests, and a short UAT checklist that covers the most-used user flows. Include tests that cover data reads, writes, and error handling. If you face slow queries, tag them in the test results and move to the tuning steps we cover later. A misconception is to only test connection success; instead verify full feature behavior and performance under representative load. For some environments you may need to update credentials to use Azure Active Directory authentication or adjust firewall rules so application hosts can reach the server. Always keep a rollback plan for the connection change so you can revert quickly if critical issues appear. Which user flow will you pick as your first UAT scenario?

keyIdea.title: Application test
keyIdea.text: Change connection endpoints, validate full feature behavior under test suites, and plan rollback options.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Update connection strings and test application functionality
Steps to validate connectivity
  1. Update the connection string to the Azure server endpoint and credentials in a test environment.
  2. Ensure firewall or Private Link rules allow the test host to reach the database.
  3. Run unit tests and integration suites that exercise reads and writes.
  4. Perform a short UAT checklist covering critical user flows and expected response times.
Pro tip

Use a staging environment with representative data to catch behavioral and performance differences before production cutover.

Connection string examples (visual only)
-- Example SQL Server connection string (visual)
Server=myazuresqlserver.database.windows.net;Database=MyDB;User Id=myuser;Password=MyPassword;

-- When switching to Azure AD auth, the authentication mechanism and credential source will change.
Update the application configuration and run tests that validate business flows, not just connectivity.
Misconception

A successful connection test is not the same as successful application behavior; always run the test suite and sample transactions.

screens.title: Indexes and statistics — first-line tuning
screens.subtitle: Rebuild indexes and update statistics to restore query performance

narration.text: One of the most effective first steps in post-migration tuning is refreshing indexes and statistics so the optimizer can produce good plans. Index fragmentation and stale statistics commonly arise after large data loads during migration. For S Q L Server, a practical sequence is to run an update statistics command for affected tables and then rebuild fragmented indexes. For PostgreSQL, run ANALYZE on the table to refresh planner statistics. MySQL offers OPTIMIZE TABLE to rebuild indexes and reclaim space. The chapter includes sample commands to run on representative tables. In addition to rebuilds, use the missing-index DMV on S Q L Server to identify index candidates by estimated impact. A misconception is to blindly create every suggested index; instead, evaluate estimated impact and trade-offs for write workloads and maintenance windows. As a concrete example, run update statistics for a critical reporting table, rebuild its indexes, rerun the slow report, and compare elapsed time. If performance improves, document the actions and consider scheduling these maintenance tasks during low-usage windows. Indexes and statistics — first-line tuning means rebuild indexes and refresh statistics to give the optimizer accurate data distribution and reduce query latency.. In practical terms, rebuild indexes and update statistics to restore query performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Index maintenance
keyIdea.text: Rebuild indexes and refresh statistics to give the optimizer accurate data distribution and reduce query latency.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Indexes and statistics — first-line tuning
Why this helps

Stale statistics and fragmented indexes cause poor execution plans. Refreshing them returns the optimizer to a known baseline and often resolves regressions.

Common commands
  • SQL Server: UPDATE STATISTICS and ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD
  • PostgreSQL: ANALYZE table
  • MySQL: OPTIMIZE TABLE
Key takeaway

Start with statistics and index maintenance before broader configuration changes.

Commands from the chapter
-- SQL Server: Rebuild an index and update statistics
ALTER INDEX ALL ON <TableName> REBUILD;
UPDATE STATISTICS <TableName>;

-- PostgreSQL: Reanalyze a table
ANALYZE <TableName>;

-- MySQL: Optimize a table
OPTIMIZE TABLE <TableName>;

-- SQL Server: missing index DMV to find candidates (visual)
SELECT dm_mid.statement AS table_name, dm_migs.avg_total_user_cost * (dm_migs.avg_user_impact / 100.0) AS estimated_impact
FROM sys.dm_db_missing_index_groups AS dm_mig
INNER JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_group_stats AS dm_migs
  ON dm_migs.group_handle = dm_mig.index_group_handle
INNER JOIN sys.dm_db_missing_index_details AS dm_mid
  ON dm_mig.index_handle = dm_mid.index_handle
WHERE dm_mid.database_id = DB_ID()
ORDER BY estimated_impact DESC;
Review suggested indexes for impact and maintenance cost before creating them.
Common mistake

Automatically creating all suggested indexes without assessing write impact and storage costs.

screens.title: Server parameters and service tier choices
screens.subtitle: Adjust engine-level settings or scale resources to match workload needs

narration.text: Performance tuning in Azure can require both database-level changes and platform adjustments. Some parameters are engine-specific: PostgreSQL administrators tune shared_buffers, work_mem, and effective_cache_size; MySQL DBAs check innodb_buffer_pool_size and query cache settings; S Q L Server DBAs review MAXDOP and cost threshold for parallelism. In addition to parameters, the selected Azure service tier and vCore count determine available C P U, memory, and input and output throughput. A practical workflow is to monitor resource utilization, identify bottlenecks, and decide whether to tune parameters or scale the tier. For example, if memory pressure is high and queries are swapping, increasing buffer sizes or moving to a higher vCore tier with more memory may be required. A misconception is to immediately scale up resources; first confirm the bottleneck and try parameter tuning or index improvements, which are often lower cost. Record any parameter changes and the observed impact, and include rollback instructions. This combined approach of tuning plus right-sizing produces the most cost-effective performance improvement. Server parameters and service tier choices means match server parameters and service tier to workload characteristics; monitor before scaling to ensure cost-effective changes.. In practical terms, adjust engine-level settings or scale resources to match workload needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Platform tuning
keyIdea.text: Match server parameters and service tier to workload characteristics; monitor before scaling to ensure cost-effective changes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Server parameters and service tier choices
Engine parameters to review
  • PostgreSQL: shared_buffers, work_mem, effective_cache_size.
  • MySQL: innodb_buffer_pool_size, query_cache_size.
  • SQL Server: MAXDOP and cost threshold for parallelism.
When to scale

Scale service tier if CPU, memory, or I/O are consistently constrained after tuning and index work.

Decision flow
  1. Monitor metrics to identify the limiting resource.
  2. Apply index and statistics fixes first to reduce unnecessary resource use.
  3. Tune engine parameters that address the observed bottleneck.
  4. If limits persist, increase vCores or switch service tier and re-evaluate.
Common mistake

Scaling before optimization; always verify whether tuning and index maintenance can resolve the issue at lower cost.

screens.title: Security hardening after migration
screens.subtitle: Restrict access, enforce strong authentication, and follow least privilege

narration.text: Securing your migrated database is non-negotiable. Begin by configuring network controls: firewall rules must restrict wide access, and for production systems prefer VNet integration or Private Link to keep traffic off the public internet. In Azure S Q L you can enable Private Link or service endpoints so only resources in an allowed subnet can reach the server. Next, verify authentication methods; consider Azure Active Directory where supported to centralize identity and control. Review logins and role assignments and remove unused accounts. Implement least-privilege authorization so applications and users only have the rights they require. A common misconception is that allowing broad IP ranges is acceptable during testing; this habit can persist and expose production systems. Finally, log and audit access attempts and configure alerts for suspicious activity such as repeated failed logins. Document network and access configurations so they are reproducible for disaster recovery and audits. Which network control will you implement first to reduce exposure? Security hardening after migration means use vnet or private link, enforce strong authentication, and apply least-privilege permissions to protect the database.. In practical terms, restrict access, enforce strong authentication, and follow least privilege. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Harden access
keyIdea.text: Use VNet or Private Link, enforce strong authentication, and apply least-privilege permissions to protect the database.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Security hardening after migration
Network protections
  • Use Private Link or VNet service endpoints to keep traffic on the Azure backbone.
  • Avoid broad firewall rules that open access from many IP ranges.
  • Allow only required subnets or specific application hosts.
Authentication

Prefer centralized identity (Azure AD) where supported, and enforce strong password and rotation policies.

Authorization & auditing

Assign roles with least privilege, remove unused accounts, and enable logging and alerts for failed logins and privilege changes.

Common mistake

Leaving temporary permissive rules in place after testing. Always lock down before production cutover.

screens.title: Monitoring, alerting, and documentation
screens.subtitle: Proactively detect regressions and keep a record of changes

narration.text: After validation and tuning, establish ongoing monitoring and alerts so you catch regressions before users notice them. Use Azure Monitor and Log Analytics to collect telemetry such as C P U utilization, storage consumption, input and output latency, and failed login events. Configure alerts for thresholds that indicate trouble, for example sustained high C P U, high input and output latency on critical disks, or sudden increase in failed logins. Use database-specific tools like Query Performance Insight for Azure S Q L to monitor expensive queries and identify regressions over time. Equally important is documentation: record the maintenance tasks you ran, the parameter changes, index creations, and the results of validation queries. That runbook becomes the authoritative guide for incident response and disaster recovery. A common misconception is that monitoring should only alert on immediate outages. Instead, configure early-warning thresholds and trend alerts so you can act before performance or security incidents escalate. End with a reflection: which metric will you monitor first to protect your critical reports? Monitoring, alerting, and documentation means use azure monitor and database telemetry to alert on resource and security anomalies, and document all post-migration actions.. In practical terms, proactively detect regressions and keep a record of changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ongoing ops
keyIdea.text: Use Azure Monitor and database telemetry to alert on resource and security anomalies, and document all post-migration actions.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › Monitoring, alerting, and documentation
Metrics to collect
  • CPU utilization and steady-state trends
  • I/O latency and throughput
  • Storage growth and free space
  • Failed login counts and audit events
Alert examples

Create alerts for sustained high CPU, high I/O latency, and sudden failed login spikes to trigger investigation.

Documentation & runbook
Record every post-migration change: indexes rebuilt, statistics updated, server parameter edits, firewall or Private Link setup, and monitoring thresholds. Include rollback steps and evidence from validation queries so future operators can reproduce or undo changes safely.
Why this matters

Documentation transforms ephemeral troubleshooting into repeatable operational practice and supports audits and disaster recovery.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from post-migration work

narration.text: These three core ideas summarize the chapter: first, data integrity validation proves that records and values were copied accurately using row counts, checksums, or sampling. Second, application functionality testing and connection string updates ensure your application actually works with the new Azure endpoint, not just that the database exists. Third, performance and security are ongoing responsibilities: rebuild indexes, update statistics, tune server parameters or scale service tiers, enforce network controls like Private Link, and configure Azure Monitor alerts. Keep documentation of every step to support rollback and audits. Remember these concepts as a compact checklist when you perform a migration: validate, test, tune, secure, and monitor. Which concept will you apply first in your environment? Key Concepts means validate data and schema, test applications, tune performance, secure access, and enable monitoring as a cohesive post-migration strategy.. In practical terms, what to remember from post-migration work. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Validate data and schema, test applications, tune performance, secure access, and enable monitoring as a cohesive post-migration strategy.

Data Integrity Validation
Verify that data was transferred without loss or corruption using counts, checksums, and aggregates.
Application Functionality Testing
Update connection strings and run unit, integration, and UAT tests to confirm end-to-end behavior.
Indexes and Statistics
Rebuild indexes and refresh statistics so the optimizer can choose efficient query plans.
Summary takeaway

Validation, tuning, security, and monitoring are a single workflow. Treat them as an operational bundle to finalize any migration.

narration.text: Keep these three concise reminders close when you finish a migration. First, validate data integrity with both counts and value-level checks; do not rely on counts alone. Second, tune the database by updating statistics, rebuilding indexes, and reviewing server parameters; check DMVs for index candidates but evaluate trade-offs before creating them. Third, secure access using VNet or Private Link and set up Azure Monitor alerts for C P U, input and output latency, storage growth, and failed logins. Record every change and the evidence it produced. These reminders will help you reduce downtime and operational surprises in production. Which reminder will you add to your post-migration checklist? Module 8 › Chapter 8.4 › What to Remember
Validate deeply
Use checksums and aggregates, not only counts, to detect subtle data issues.
Tune deliberately
Refresh statistics and indexes first; then tune parameters or scale the service tier if needed.
Monitor continuously
Set alerts for CPU, I/O latency, storage, and failed logins to detect regressions early.
Final takeaway

Treat post-migration work as an operational handoff: validate, tune, secure, and document every change.
